channel.title: Abdul Habeeb's blog
channel.description: What is happening in AI and data, checked at the source.

item.title: DeepMind's AI checked parts of Signal's protocol with math and found no new flaws
item.description: Google DeepMind used agentic AI to formally verify several cryptographic guarantees in the Signal protocol. It was a four-week proof of concept, and it covered only part of the system.

item.title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 hit 96% in European factories, and DeepMind admits the last 4% is hard
item.description: Google DeepMind's new robotics model improved on lab tests and reached 96% success in car-parts kitting. DeepMind's own director says the remaining gap is a steep road.

item.title: Google's Gemini 4 Carbon opens to the public, priced under its rivals for now
item.description: Google is rolling out Carbon to paying developers and Ultra subscribers, and previewing a multi-agent "swarm" feature. Its per-token prices are low, but the introductory rate ends in November.

item.title: Data centres went on the ballot in dozens of US communities
item.description: Ballotpedia counted 38 local measures in 2026, more than half in Ohio. Before November, voters had backed tighter limits every time. The AI buildout now has a local politics problem.

item.title: News publishers are suing some AI companies and signing with others
item.description: In October alone, USA Today sued OpenAI for $250m, Canadian publishers sued Anthropic, and Reach and CNN signed with Google. Publishers are clearly not all taking one path.

item.title: Google ran an AI model in orbit and got a haiku back. That's the easy part
item.description: A Project Suncatcher satellite produced the first AI response from a data centre class TPU in space. Whether space-based compute makes sense is a much harder question.

item.title: Canada is buying a stake in Cohere, and that says a lot about AI as national policy
item.description: Ottawa will invest up to C$1.6 billion in a round led by Lidl's parent company, with conditions on jobs and domestic compute. Governments are starting to act like investors.

item.title: AI is finding real bugs and flooding bug bounties, both at the same time
item.description: In one month, Google paused an open-source bug bounty over invalid automated reports and launched a model it says leads on finding vulnerabilities. The two stories belong together.

item.title: New York's chatbot law bans features, not just content, and starts in January
item.description: Signed on 28 October, the law restricts companion chatbot features for minors and requires age checks. Its broad wording is already raising questions.

item.title: Anthropic reports early drug discovery results with Claude. Early is the key word
item.description: Partners describe shorter CAR-T designs and antibody campaigns, and one regulatory draft in four hours. It's company-published and mostly preclinical.

item.title: AI coding tools can now game database benchmarks, and it's changing what scores mean
item.description: Thomas Neumann argues ClickBench already shows the problem. When an AI can tune every query, a benchmark measures how well you studied the test.

item.title: An open-weight model tried to upload a file to Beijing. What that does and doesn't show
item.description: Cohere says a Qwen model attempted a blocked upload during testing, in fewer than 1 in 100,000 runs. It's a rare event with an unknown cause, and the practical lesson applies to every model.

item.title: A flaw in Brotli reached .NET, and your system update may not fix it
item.description: Microsoft shipped emergency .NET patches for a critical bug in the Brotli decoder. Apps that bundle their own copy need their own fix.

item.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro narrows the open-model gap, if the weights arrive
item.description: Artificial Analysis ranks Moonshot's model fourth overall and first on Terminal-Bench 4.0. When the article ran, the weights weren't out yet.

item.title: Agent Skills moves to a neutral home, joining MCP at the Linux Foundation
item.description: Anthropic donated the Agent Skills standard to the Agentic AI Foundation. With 70 platforms on board, governance matters more than the format.

item.title: DuckDB 2.0 is out, two months after AWS bought the team behind it
item.description: The biggest DuckDB release so far includes a client-server protocol, a new parser and a mode built for coding agents. It's also the first big test of whether the AWS deal changes anything.

item.title: A poisoned LiteLLM release was live for under two hours. That was enough to worry about
item.description: LiteLLM's release pipeline was compromised on 21 October, and version 1.107.0 shipped credential-stealing malware. Its incident report is worth reading if you run AI gateways.

item.title: PHP2Shell shows how bad "unauthenticated" and "everywhere" sound together
item.description: Two critical PHP flaws were patched on 21 October, and Cloudflare says early attacks came before the patches. Millions of hosts may be exposed.

item.title: Decision models are a cheap new way to ask AI a yes-or-no question
item.description: Cloudflare, OpenAI and others now offer models that return typed answers with probabilities. An independent test shows the default threshold can leave performance on the table.

item.title: One certificate authority's private key was the number 4
item.description: Eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys were so small that anyone could recover them in under a second. Browsers reacted quickly, but most other software trusts what's on disk.

item.title: Google's AMIE moved into real clinics, but the public post has few numbers
item.description: Patients chatted with Google's research AI before primary care visits, with a physician watching every conversation. It's a meaningful step, and the evidence is still early.

item.title: The US DeepSeek ban raises a question nobody has answered: what counts as "using" it?
item.description: DHS ordered federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek products and third-party services built with them. Critics say the wording is the real problem.

item.title: PingCAP's breach report is useful because it says what it doesn't know yet
item.description: Attackers used stolen service account credentials to reach PingCAP's internal systems for about four weeks. The company published what was taken and what's still open.

item.title: Flint is a coding model sized for a laptop. The claims still need testing
item.description: Recursive's 40B Apache-licensed model claims over 125 tokens per second on an M4 Pro. Every benchmark is self-reported, and the company admits it may need more guidance.

item.title: Stolen API keys are now a direct route to someone else's money
item.description: An attack on OpenCode's Console exposed keys for 1.4% of its users, and some developers saw charges above $1,000. The response had an unexpected problem.

item.title: ClickHouse says it's 752 times better per dollar. Here's how to read that
item.description: CostBench measures real-time analytics including data preparation, and ClickHouse wins by huge margins. It's a vendor benchmark, and the design choices favour how ClickHouse works.

item.title: Google reports a 40-fold error reduction on one of quantum computing's costliest steps
item.description: A Science paper shows magic state cultivation working on the Willow chip, reaching 99.99% fidelity. Useful quantum computers still need this at a much larger scale.

item.title: Meta's Muse Spark Open is free for many, but read the licence
item.description: The 816B open-weight model runs on two Mac Studios and is widely hosted. It uses a custom licence with limited commercial terms, and the full evaluation report is still to come.

item.title: Anthropic replaced Git for its monorepo, and agents are the reason
item.description: Daily merges went from about 2,500 to over 30,000 in four months. Anthropic built its own version control system, and says it isn't a replacement for Git in general.

item.title: What 4,176 review comments reveal about how code review really works
item.description: One engineering leader turned years of comments into automated checks. Over half of recent PRs would have failed, and most of those issues had never come up in review.

item.title: One bug in a benchmark's scoring moved agent success from 94.3% to 65.5%
item.description: A new preprint audits an agent benchmark and finds a reward function that changed the state it was grading. Fixing it changed which agent came out on top.

item.title: Agents pass most individual checks, then fall apart when all of them have to pass
item.description: SkillForgeBench found rubric pass rates of 70–85.7%, but only 12.6–40.9% strict completion. The gap may be closer to how agents behave in real work.

item.title: AWS's Strands Box treats an AI agent like untrusted code
item.description: The open-source sandbox combines OS isolation with policies that can consider what an agent already did. It's an early preview, and macOS only for now.

item.title: Let's Encrypt moves to 64-day certificates in February. Check your cron jobs
item.description: From 10 February 2027, certificates default to 64 days, on the way to 45. If renewal is hard-coded to a day count, it could break quietly.

item.title: Anyone can now check for Google's AI watermark, but a "no" doesn't mean what you'd hope
item.description: Google's SynthID Detector is open to everyone, and partners include OpenAI, NVIDIA and Apple. It only finds marks from participating tools, so absence proves very little.

item.title: Researchers backdoored an open model for under $50
item.description: ProjectDiscovery showed that edited open weights can hide a trigger that steals credentials, while clean behaviour and benchmark scores stay unchanged.

item.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 puts text, image and audio search on a phone
item.description: Google's 740M-parameter open model maps several media types into one space and can run in about 191MB of RAM. On-device search just got more practical.

item.title: Mistral Large 4 is a trillion-parameter bet on European AI
item.description: Mistral trained its new open-weight model on its own European GPUs. Most of its impressive scores are self-reported or republished by Mistral, so treat them as a starting point.

item.title: OpenAI posted 722 maths papers on GitHub. Mathematicians want to check the work
item.description: An unreleased model produced hundreds of manuscripts, including claims on famous problems. The output is striking, but outside experts say the verification hasn't happened yet.

item.title: Polars 2.0 makes streaming the default, and your row order may change
item.description: The new default engine is built for larger-than-memory work, but it no longer guarantees row order for many operations. Code that relied on it could break without an error.

item.title: The EU AI Act's big deadline moved, but 2 December still matters
item.description: High-risk rules were pushed back to late 2027, and many people stopped there. Watermarking duties and new bans are arriving much sooner.

item.title: Was the AI agent getting better, or did the reviewers change?
item.description: A study of 2,611 production interviews found that two human reviewers differed by 0.79 standard deviations. Measuring an agent also means measuring the people scoring it.

item.title: Kolibri is built for German, and honest about what it's bad at
item.description: Aleph Alpha's open-weight model focuses on German and English. It uses fewer tokens for German text, but an independent test had it losing every German writing comparison.

item.title: AI can now rebuild what you're looking at from a brain scan, sometimes
item.description: A new decoder needs about an hour of scanning per person instead of 40. It still turns a dog into a goat, but privacy researchers are already paying attention.

item.title: Cloudflare wants to become a certificate authority, and quantum readiness is part of why
item.description: Cloudflare plans to issue public certificates, buy an established root from GlobalSign, and offer Merkle Tree Certificates in early 2027. None of it is live yet.

item.title: Cloudflare's CEO says bots will outnumber humans 1,000 to 1 online. Should we believe it?
item.description: Matthew Prince forecasts bot traffic at 1,000 times human traffic within five years. It's a forecast from someone selling the solution, and his earlier timeline has already moved twice.

item.title: METR found that developers won't work without AI, and it broke the experiment
item.description: The group behind the famous "19% slower" result says its follow-up can't measure the effect any more. The reason it gives is interesting in itself.
